## Essential Problem:

The essential problem is that the standard DID estimator is biased when the parallel trends assumption is violated, even if the violation is small. In the specific case presented, wages in OH are higher than wages in IN for a short period before the treatment. This pre-existing difference can lead to an overestimation of the treatment effect if not accounted for.

## Relevant Information:

* **Nature of the Pre-existing Difference:** We need to understand the nature of the pre-existing difference and its potential causes. Is it a one-time event or a persistent trend? Is it related to the treatment in any way?
* **Magnitude of the Pre-existing Difference:** The magnitude of the pre-existing difference relative to the expected treatment effect is crucial. A small difference might not significantly impact the results, while a large difference could render the DID estimates unreliable.
* **Data Availability:** The availability of data for periods before the treatment is essential. Longer pre-treatment periods provide more information about the trends and allow for a more robust analysis.

## Potential Solutions:

* **Controlling for Pre-existing Differences:** We can include additional control variables in the DID model to account for the pre-existing difference. These variables could be time-varying factors that explain the difference in wages between OH and IN before the treatment.
* **Using Alternative Estimators:** Several alternative estimators have been proposed to address violations of the parallel trends assumption. These include the synthetic control method, the event study approach, and the difference-in-differences-in-differences (DDD) estimator.
* **Sensitivity Analysis:** Conducting a sensitivity analysis can help assess the impact of the pre-existing difference on the DID estimates. This involves varying the assumptions about the pre-existing difference and observing how the results change.

## Addressing the User's Query:

While there aren't many papers directly addressing small pre-treatment differences, the mentioned paper on "Honest Parallel Trends" offers insights. Although it focuses on post-treatment trends, the underlying principle of controlling for pre-existing differences remains relevant.

In this specific case, including an additional control variable representing the pre-existing difference (i.e., the wage gap in OH during the period 𝑇=−5−𝑘,−5 ) could potentially adjust for the bias. However, this approach relies on the assumption that the pre-existing difference is unrelated to the treatment effect. 

Further exploration of alternative estimators like synthetic control and DDD, along with sensitivity analysis to gauge the impact of the pre-existing difference on the estimates, would be beneficial.

It's important to acknowledge that addressing small violations of parallel trends is an ongoing challenge in the DID literature. While there's no definitive answer, employing various techniques and carefully considering the context can help researchers obtain more reliable estimates.
gold_answer:
$\begingroup$

If you have violations of the parallel trend assumption then you will have
biased estimates of the causal effect (assuming you satisfy the other
assumptions). If you know the maximum that the two series can drift apart over
time or have a functional form that specifies how that difference can arise,
then you can estimate the diff in diff in a bounded way. For example, if IN
has a trend of 2% growth per year and OH has a trend growth of 3%, then adding
a linear time variable to a log regression will result in parallel trends.

You don't need the trends to be identical. Effectively, you need them to be
identical in expectation (see Lechner (2011) [ The Estimation of Causal
Effects by Difference-in-Difference Methods
](https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/6387069.pdf) ). [ ![Common Trend as an
expectation from Lechner \(2011\)](https://i.sstatic.net/u34uD.png)
](https://i.sstatic.net/u34uD.png)

What I did in my paper, [ Competition and complementarities in retail banking:
Evidence from debit card interchange regulation
](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1042957318300184) , is
look at the trends in the pre-treatment period and test if they were
statistically distinguishable. [ ![testing common trend in pre
period](https://i.sstatic.net/qjmHd.jpg) ](https://i.sstatic.net/qjmHd.jpg) .
Of course, you can never test that the common trend in the pre-period would
persist in the counterfactual treatment period in the absence of the
treatment. That can only be assumed.

Another approach is to do a [ synthetic cohort
](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_control_method) analysis. Basically,
you construct a fake control for each treated unit out of linear combinations
of control units to maximize the similarity between control and treated units.
You can do that in a way that closely or even exactly matches the pre-
treatment trend of the treatment and control groups.
